questions.prompt: You are applying a force vector v = [5, 0] to an object, representing a 5 m/s push to the right. If you scale this vector by -2, what is the resulting motion of the object?
options: A 10 m/s push to the right
A 10 m/s push to the left
A 2.5 m/s push to the left
A 5 m/s push to the left
questions.explanation: Scalar multiplication by -2 doubles the magnitude (from 5 to 10) and the negative sign flips the direction 180 degrees, changing rightward motion to leftward motion.
correctAnswers: A 10 m/s push to the left

image.alt: Diagram illustrating the tip-to-tail and parallelogram methods of vector addition.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements accurately describe the geometric 'Tip-to-Tail' method of vector addition?
options: The resultant vector is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the tip of the second.
The order of addition changes the final destination point.
It represents the cumulative effect of two different displacements.
It requires both vectors to start at the origin simultaneously.
It can be visualized as forming a parallelogram where the diagonal is the sum.
questions.explanation: Vector addition is commutative (order doesn't matter) and the Tip-to-Tail method shows how displacements combine. The Parallelogram Law is a related visualization of the same result.
correctAnswers: The resultant vector is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the tip of the second.
It represents the cumulative effect of two different displacements.
It can be visualized as forming a parallelogram where the diagonal is the sum.

questions.prompt: In the context of linear algebra operations, multiplying a vector by a single number is often referred to as ____ because it changes the magnitude of the vector while keeping it on the same line of action.
questions.explanation: Scaling describes how a scalar stretches, shrinks, or reverses a vector's length without rotating it off its original span or line.
correctAnswers: scaling
scalar multiplication

questions.prompt: If an image is treated as a high-dimensional vector of pixel values, which operation would effectively increase the brightness of the entire image?
options: Subtracting a constant vector from the image vector
Scaling the image vector by a factor greater than 1
Scaling the image vector by a factor between 0 and 1
Adding two different image vectors together
questions.explanation: Scaling the entire vector by a number > 1 increases every individual pixel value (component) proportionally, which results in a brighter image.
correctAnswers: Scaling the image vector by a factor greater than 1

questions.prompt: Why does the resultant vector's length change as the angle between the two added vectors increases from 0 to 180 degrees?
options: Because the vectors begin to oppose each other, causing their individual magnitudes to cancel out.
Because scaling one vector automatically reduces the magnitude of the second vector.
Because the coordinate system rotates to compensate for the change in direction.
Because the tail of the second vector is being moved further away from the origin.
questions.explanation: When vectors point in the same direction (0°), their magnitudes add perfectly. As they move toward opposite directions (180°), they work against each other, reducing the net displacement.
questions.animationHtml:

correctAnswers: Because the vectors begin to oppose each other, causing their individual magnitudes to cancel out.

questions.prompt: You are given two vectors, v and w, that are not multiples of each other. If you use a weight of zero for v and a weight of 5 for w, what geometric object describes the set of all resulting vectors if you were to vary the weight of w while keeping v's weight at zero?
options: A single point at the origin
A line passing through the origin
A 2D plane in 3D space
A curved path across the grid
questions.explanation: By keeping the weight of v at zero, you are only scaling w. The set of all scalar multiples of a single non-zero vector forms a line that passes through the origin.
correctAnswers: A line passing through the origin

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements accurately describe the 'span' of a set of vectors?
options: It is the set of all possible linear combinations of those vectors.
It represents the 'reach' or 'coverage' of those vectors in space.
It is only valid if the weights used are positive integers.
If a target vector is in the span, it can be built using those vectors as instructions.
The span of any two vectors is always a 3D volume.
questions.explanation: Span includes all linear combinations using any real-valued weights (negative, zero, or fractional). While the span of two vectors can be a plane, it is not a 3D volume, and it can even be a line if the vectors are collinear.
correctAnswers: It is the set of all possible linear combinations of those vectors.
It represents the 'reach' or 'coverage' of those vectors in space.
If a target vector is in the span, it can be built using those vectors as instructions.

image.alt: A 3D diagram showing a target vector pointing away from the plane spanned by two other vectors.

questions.prompt: Consider two vectors in 3D space that do not point in the same direction. If a third 'target' vector cannot be reached by any linear combination of the first two, what does this imply geometrically?
options: The target vector lies on the plane formed by the first two vectors.
The target vector pokes out of the infinite sheet of paper formed by the first two.
The target vector is the zero vector.
The first two vectors are actually the same vector.
questions.explanation: The span of two non-collinear vectors in 3D is a 2D plane. If a vector cannot be formed by their combination, it must have a component in a direction that the plane does not cover.
correctAnswers: The target vector pokes out of the infinite sheet of paper formed by the first two.

questions.prompt: If you are solving the equation x(v) + y(w) = t to see if vector 't' is in the span of 'v' and 'w', which outcomes are possible for the scalars x and y?
options: There is exactly one unique pair of values for x and y.
There are no possible values for x and y.
There are infinitely many solutions if v and w are collinear and t lies on that line.
The values for x and y must always be identical.
questions.explanation: If 't' is outside the span, there are no solutions. If 'v' and 'w' are independent and 't' is in the span, there is one unique solution. If 'v' and 'w' point the same way, there can be infinite ways to sum them to 't'.
correctAnswers: There is exactly one unique pair of values for x and y.
There are no possible values for x and y.
There are infinitely many solutions if v and w are collinear and t lies on that line.

questions.prompt: Observe the target vector and the two basis vectors. As the weights for the basis vectors are adjusted, why is the target vector eventually unreachable even when the weights become very large?
options: Because the target vector has a vertical component that the two basis vectors, which lie flat, cannot replicate.
Because the basis vectors are shrinking as the weights increase, preventing them from reaching the target.
Because linear combinations can only reach points that are whole-number multiples of the basis vectors.
Because the target vector is rotating away from the basis vectors faster than they can grow.
questions.explanation: If the target vector lies outside the 2D plane (span) created by the two basis vectors, no amount of scaling or adding (linear combination) can ever reach it because the basis vectors lack the 'upward' dimension.

correctAnswers: Because the target vector has a vertical component that the two basis vectors, which lie flat, cannot replicate.

questions.prompt: If a set of vectors is linearly dependent, what does this imply about the 'information' they provide in a space?
options: Every vector in the set can be created by a combination of the others.
At least one vector in the set adds no new dimensions to the span of the others.
The vectors must all be multiples of one another.
The vectors are at right angles to each other, maximizing efficiency.
questions.explanation: Linear dependence means there is redundancy; at least one vector lies within the span of the others, meaning it doesn't extend the reachable 'territory' or add a new dimension.
correctAnswers: At least one vector in the set adds no new dimensions to the span of the others.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conditions satisfy the definition of a set of vectors {v₁, v₂, v₃} being linearly independent?
options: The only solution to c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + c₃v₃ = 0 is c₁ = c₂ = c₃ = 0.
No vector in the set can be expressed as a linear combination of the others.
The vectors are all orthogonal (at 90-degree angles) to each other.
The span of the vectors is a line in 3D space.
One vector is the sum of the other two.
questions.explanation: Independence requires that the 'trivial solution' is the only solution to the linear combination equation. This geometrically implies that no vector is redundant (cannot be built from the others). Orthogonality implies independence, but it is not a requirement for it.
correctAnswers: The only solution to c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + c₃v₃ = 0 is c₁ = c₂ = c₃ = 0.
No vector in the set can be expressed as a linear combination of the others.

questions.prompt: In the context of data compression, we look for linearly ____ vectors because they represent redundant information that can be discarded without losing the essence of the data.
correctAnswers: dependent

image.alt: A diagram of two vectors on a 2D plane within 3D space, with a third vector pointing outside that plane.

questions.prompt: You have two vectors forming a plane in 3D space. If you add a third vector that is NOT on that plane, what is the status of the new set of three vectors?
options: The set is linearly dependent because they are in 3D space.
The set is linearly independent because the third vector adds a new dimension.
The set is linearly dependent because the first two vectors already defined a span.
The set is orthogonal because the third vector points away from the plane.
questions.explanation: Since the third vector points 'out' of the plane created by the first two, it cannot be formed by any combination of them. This adds a third dimension to the span, making the set independent.
correctAnswers: The set is linearly independent because the third vector adds a new dimension.

questions.prompt: Watch the third vector (green) change its orientation. Why does the 'Independent' status light switch to 'Dependent' at a specific moment?
options: Because the green vector becomes the same length as the red vector.
Because the green vector falls into the shaded span created by the red and blue vectors.
Because the green vector reaches a 90-degree angle relative to the blue vector.
Because the green vector is rotating at a constant velocity.
questions.explanation: Independence is lost the moment a vector becomes redundant. In the animation, as soon as the green vector lies flat on the plane (span) formed by the other two, it no longer provides a new direction of travel.

questions.prompt: If a subspace is defined as a flat plane passing through the origin in 3D space (R³), what is the dimension of this subspace?
options: It depends on the orientation of the plane
questions.explanation: The dimension of a subspace is the number of vectors in any of its bases. A plane is a two-dimensional object because it requires exactly two linearly independent vectors to span it, regardless of the dimension of the 'ambient' space it sits in.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conditions MUST be met for a set of vectors to be considered a 'Basis' for a specific vector space?
options: The vectors must be mutually orthogonal (at 90 degree angles).
The vectors must be linearly independent.
The vectors must span the entire space.
The number of vectors must exceed the dimension of the space.
The vectors must all be unit vectors (length of 1).
questions.explanation: A basis is defined by two criteria: it must span the space (reach every point) and be linearly independent (contain no redundant information). While orthogonality and unit length are properties of 'orthonormal' bases, they are not requirements for a general basis.
correctAnswers: The vectors must be linearly independent.
The vectors must span the entire space.

questions.prompt: In a 4-dimensional space, any basis for that space must contain exactly ____ vectors.
questions.explanation: The dimension of a space and the number of vectors in its basis are the same by definition. If a space is 4D, any set of vectors that both spans it and is independent must have exactly 4 vectors.
correctAnswers: four

questions.prompt: You are given three vectors in R³. You find that the third vector can be written as the sum of the first two. What can you conclude about this set of vectors?
options: They form a basis for R³.
They are linearly independent.
They span a 2D subspace (a plane) but not the full R³.
They have a dimension of 3.
questions.explanation: Because the third vector is a combination of the others, the set is linearly dependent. In R³, you need three linearly independent vectors to form a basis. Here, only two are independent, meaning they span a 2D plane.
correctAnswers: They span a 2D subspace (a plane) but not the full R³.

questions.prompt: As the simulation adjusts the direction of the second vector to align perfectly with the first, why does the 'Spanned Region' suddenly collapse from a plane to a line?
options: Because the vectors become longer, they can no longer fit in a 2D representation.
Because the set loses linear independence, meaning the vectors no longer provide the second 'direction' needed to cover a plane.
Because the dimension of the ambient space (R³) was reduced by the user's interaction.
Because two vectors can only ever span a line regardless of their orientation.
questions.explanation: A basis for a plane requires two independent directions. When vectors become collinear (parallel), they become linearly dependent, and their span drops to 1D because one vector is just a multiple of the other.
questions.animationHtml:

correctAnswers: Because the set loses linear independence, meaning the vectors no longer provide the second 'direction' needed to cover a plane.

questions.prompt: In a system of three linear equations with variables x, y, and z, what does a value of '0' in the second column of the augmented matrix signify?
options: The entire second equation is equal to zero.
The variable y is absent from that specific equation.
The solution for the variable y must be zero.
The system has no intersection point at y = 0.
questions.explanation: Since each column in an augmented matrix corresponds to a specific variable, a zero indicates that the variable for that column has a coefficient of zero in that particular constraint (equation).
correctAnswers: The variable y is absent from that specific equation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are true regarding the 'vertical bar' commonly drawn inside an augmented matrix?
options: It serves as a visual substitute for the equals signs in the linear system.
It separates the coefficients of the variables from the constant terms.
It indicates that the matrix must be multiplied by another vector.
It divides the 'rules' of the system from the 'results' or constraints.
questions.explanation: The vertical bar is a bookkeeping tool used to distinguish the coefficient matrix (the left side) from the constants (the right side), mirroring the structure of the original equations.
correctAnswers: It serves as a visual substitute for the equals signs in the linear system.
It separates the coefficients of the variables from the constant terms.
It divides the 'rules' of the system from the 'results' or constraints.

questions.prompt: If a factory's resource constraints are modeled such that each row of an augmented matrix represents a specific resource, then each ____ represents the 'signature' or requirements of a single product across all resources.
questions.explanation: In this modeling perspective, a column tracks how one specific variable (or product) impacts every different constraint (row) in the system.
correctAnswers: column

image.alt: A diagram illustrating the mapping of coefficients from unaligned equations into a structured matrix format.

questions.prompt: When translating a 'messy' system of equations into a matrix, why is it essential to maintain strict alignment of the variables first?
options: To ensure the matrix is square (equal rows and columns).
Because the matrix relies on position rather than labels to identify variables.
To prevent the constants from becoming negative during translation.
So that the vertical bar can be placed in the center of the matrix.
questions.explanation: Matrices strip away variable labels (x, y, z). Therefore, the physical column position is the only way the math 'remembers' which coefficient belongs to which variable.
correctAnswers: Because the matrix relies on position rather than labels to identify variables.

questions.prompt: As the system of equations is transformed into an augmented matrix, why is the resulting numerical grid considered a 'map of dependencies'?
options: Because each row demonstrates how a single constraint is built from different variable inputs.
Because the total number of cells in the grid is always equal to the number of variables squared.
Because the vertical bar ensures that the variables on the left side are always larger than the constants.
Because the zeros in the matrix indicate that the variables are completely independent of each other.
questions.explanation: The matrix represents how each constraint (row) depends on the weighted contribution of various variables (columns). The animation shows this 'stripping' of labels to reveal the underlying numerical structure of these relationships.
questions.animationHtml:
Animation showing the transition from a 3D linear system to an augmented matrix.

System of linear equations transforming into an augmented matrix
correctAnswers: Because each row demonstrates how a single constraint is built from different variable inputs.

questions.prompt: In a system of linear equations reduced to RREF, what specifically determines whether a variable is categorized as 'free'?
options: The variable corresponds to a column that does not contain a leading 1 (pivot).
The variable is located in the last column of the augmented matrix.
The variable has a coefficient of zero in every single equation of the original system.
The variable can be solved for directly without referencing any other variables.
questions.explanation: In RREF, pivot columns identify basic (dependent) variables. Any column in the coefficient matrix that lacks a pivot corresponds to a free variable, meaning it can take on any value, which then determines the values of the pivot variables.
correctAnswers: The variable corresponds to a column that does not contain a leading 1 (pivot).

questions.prompt: Suppose you have a system of 3 equations with 5 variables, and its RREF form has pivots in columns 1, 2, and 4. Which of the following statements are true about the solution set?
options: There are exactly two free variables.
The solution set forms a 2D plane in 5D space.
Variables x3 and x5 are the free variables.
The system has a unique solution because there are three pivots.
The parametric vector form will involve two parameter-scaled vectors.
questions.explanation: With 5 variables and 3 pivots, there are 5 - 3 = 2 free variables (x3 and x5). Each free variable becomes a parameter in the vector form, and the number of free variables defines the dimension (2D plane) of the solution space.
correctAnswers: There are exactly two free variables.
The solution set forms a 2D plane in 5D space.
Variables x3 and x5 are the free variables.
The parametric vector form will involve two parameter-scaled vectors.

questions.prompt: If a consistent linear system results in a solution set that geometrically represents a line in 3D space, the number of free variables in the system must be ____.
questions.explanation: The number of free variables corresponds to the dimensionality of the solution set. A line is a 1-dimensional object, therefore it requires exactly one free variable (parameter) to describe.
correctAnswers: one

image.alt: Geometric representation of a parametric line equation.

questions.prompt: When converting a system from RREF equations to parametric vector form, what do the constant terms (those not associated with a free variable) represent?
options: A position vector that shifts the solution set away from the origin.
The direction in which the solution set extends infinitely.
The number of free variables present in the system.
The specific values of the free variables when the pivot variables are zero.
questions.explanation: The constant vector in parametric form is a specific solution to the system. It acts as a 'base point' or 'anchor' in space, while the vectors multiplied by parameters provide the 'directions' of the solution set.
correctAnswers: A position vector that shifts the solution set away from the origin.

questions.prompt: As the value of the parameter 's' changes while 't' remains fixed, why does the point representing the solution move along a straight line rather than jumping randomly?
options: Because 's' scales a fixed direction vector, creating a continuous linear path from the starting point.
Because the system is in RREF, which forces all solutions to be equidistant from the origin.
Because 't' acts as a pivot, locking the variable 's' into a specific coordinate plane.
Because free variables can only represent integer values in a parametric solution set.
questions.explanation: In parametric vector form, each free variable (parameter) is multiplied by a constant vector. Changing one parameter while holding others constant is equivalent to moving in the direction of that parameter's associated vector.

correctAnswers: Because 's' scales a fixed direction vector, creating a continuous linear path from the starting point.

sessions.title: Rank, Consistency, and the Number of Solutions

image.alt: Matrix showing an inconsistent system with a row of zeros equal to 5.

questions.prompt: If a 3x3 matrix $A$ in a system $Ax = b$ has a row of all zeros after Gaussian elimination, but the corresponding entry in the augmented column is 5, what can you conclude about the system?
options: The system has a unique solution.
The system is inconsistent and has no solution.
The system has infinitely many solutions.
The system's rank is 3.
questions.explanation: A row of [0 0 0 | 5] represents the equation 0 = 5, which is a contradiction. This occurs when the rank of the augmented matrix is greater than the rank of the coefficient matrix.
correctAnswers: The system is inconsistent and has no solution.

questions.prompt: Under which conditions will a consistent system of linear equations $Ax = b$ with $n$ variables have infinitely many solutions?
options: The rank of the coefficient matrix is equal to $n$.
The rank of the coefficient matrix is less than $n$.
There is at least one free variable in the system.
The rank of the augmented matrix is greater than the rank of the coefficient matrix.
questions.explanation: Infinitely many solutions occur when a system is consistent but there is 'freedom' (free variables), which happens when the rank (number of pivots) is less than the number of variables.
correctAnswers: The rank of the coefficient matrix is less than $n$.
There is at least one free variable in the system.

questions.prompt: The ____ of a matrix is defined as the number of pivots in its row echelon form, representing the number of independent pieces of information in the system.
questions.explanation: Rank measures the 'useful' information or independent rows/columns in a matrix. It is found by counting the non-zero rows (pivots) in row echelon form.
correctAnswers: rank

questions.prompt: According to the Rouché-Capelli Theorem, a system is consistent if and only if:
options: The rank of A equals the rank of the augmented matrix [A|b].
The rank of A is equal to the number of variables.
The determinant of A is non-zero.
The matrix A is in reduced row echelon form.
questions.explanation: Consistency means a solution exists. This happens when the result vector 'b' does not increase the rank of the matrix, meaning it lies within the reach of the matrix columns.
correctAnswers: The rank of A equals the rank of the augmented matrix [A|b].

questions.prompt: Why does the intersection point disappear and then reappear as a whole line when the slope of one equation is adjusted to match the other?
options: Because the rank of the augmented matrix suddenly exceeds the number of variables.
Because the system transitions from a unique solution to an inconsistent state, and finally to a state where the equations are redundant.
Because the number of variables changes as the lines become parallel.
Because the determinant of the system becomes larger than the rank of the coefficient matrix.
questions.explanation: As slopes align, the system loses rank. If the lines are parallel but separated, they are inconsistent (no solution). If they overlap, they are redundant (rank < n), creating infinite solutions.

Animated geometry of two lines in a coordinate plane

Line 1 Slope fixed 0.50
Line 2 Slope 1.20
Line 1 Intercept fixed 0.00
Line 2 Intercept 40.00
Geometry of a 2-equation linear system across varying parameters.
correctAnswers: Because the system transitions from a unique solution to an inconsistent state, and finally to a state where the equations are redundant.

sessions.title: Column Space and the Geometry of Ax = b

questions.prompt: In the equation Ax = b, what role do the entries of the vector x play when viewing the operation through the 'Column Picture'?
options: They represent the dot product result of each row with the target vector b.
They act as weights or instructions for how much of each column in A to combine.
They define the dimensions of the subspace containing the origin.
They represent the angles between the column vectors of matrix A.
questions.explanation: In the column picture, Ax is viewed as a linear combination of the columns of A. The components of x are the scalars (weights) that determine how much of each column vector is contributed to the final sum.
correctAnswers: They act as weights or instructions for how much of each column in A to combine.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements are true regarding the Column Space C(A) of a matrix A?
options: C(A) consists of all possible linear combinations of the columns of A.
The system Ax = b is solvable if and only if b is an element of C(A).
The number of rows in A always determines the dimension of C(A).
C(A) is the 'reach' or 'capability' of the matrix to form vectors b.
A solution exists even if b is outside the span of the columns.
questions.explanation: C(A) is defined as the span (all combinations) of the columns. For Ax=b to have a solution, b must be 'reachable' by those columns, meaning it lies within that span. The number of rows determines the space b lives in, but not necessarily the dimension of the column space itself.
correctAnswers: C(A) consists of all possible linear combinations of the columns of A.
The system Ax = b is solvable if and only if b is an element of C(A).
C(A) is the 'reach' or 'capability' of the matrix to form vectors b.

questions.prompt: If a 3x2 matrix has columns that are multiples of each other, its column space in 3D space is geometrically a ____.
correctAnswers: line
straight line

image.alt: A 3D diagram showing a vector b pointing away from the 2D plane formed by the matrix columns.

questions.prompt: Consider a 3x2 matrix A. If we try to solve Ax = b and find that it is an 'Impossible System' via Gaussian elimination, what is the geometric relationship between b and C(A)?
options: Vector b is the zero vector and lies at the origin of C(A).
Vector b lies exactly on the 2D plane formed by the columns of A.
Vector b points in a direction that lies outside the 2D plane spanned by the columns.
Vector b is parallel to the first column but perpendicular to the second.
questions.explanation: An impossible system (0=1 contradiction) occurs geometrically when the target vector b is not in the column space. For a 3x2 matrix, the column space is at most a 2D plane; if b is outside this plane, no combination of columns can ever reach it.
correctAnswers: Vector b points in a direction that lies outside the 2D plane spanned by the columns.

questions.prompt: As we vary the scalar weights x1 and x2 in the simulation, why is the resulting vector Ax confined to the shaded region?
options: Because the columns of A are restricted to a single plane, any linear combination of them must also reside in that same plane.
Because the weights x1 and x2 are required to sum to one, preventing the vector from leaving the surface.
Because the matrix A has more rows than columns, which automatically forces the output into a lower-dimensional coordinate system.
Because the columns of A are perpendicular to one another, which locks the resulting vector into a fixed grid.
questions.explanation: The animation shows that no matter how large or small we make the weights, the resulting vector Ax never leaves the flat plane. This is because the columns act as the only two 'available directions,' and you cannot create a third dimension of movement out of only two basis directions.

questions.prompt: If a 3x3 matrix has a rank of 2, what is the geometric representation of its null space in the 3D input space?
options: A single point at the origin
A line passing through the origin
A plane passing through the origin
The entire 3D space
questions.explanation: The dimension of the null space (nullity) is equal to the number of columns minus the rank (3 - 2 = 1). A one-dimensional subspace in 3D is geometrically represented as a line passing through the origin.
correctAnswers: A line passing through the origin

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements correctly describe the relationship between a matrix A and its null space N(A)?
options: The null space is always a subspace of the domain (input space).
The zero vector is always a member of the null space.
If the null space contains only the zero vector, the matrix columns must be linearly dependent.
The number of free variables in the RREF of A determines the dimension of the null space.
The null space is the set of all vectors b such that Ax = b has a solution.
questions.explanation: The null space exists in the input space and always includes the trivial solution (zero). Its dimension is exactly the number of free variables found during Gaussian elimination. The set of reachable b vectors is actually the column space, not the null space.
correctAnswers: The null space is always a subspace of the domain (input space).
The zero vector is always a member of the null space.
The number of free variables in the RREF of A determines the dimension of the null space.

questions.prompt: In linear algebra, the null space is also frequently referred to by the synonym ____.
correctAnswers: kernel

questions.prompt: If a 10x10 matrix A has 10 pivots, what can be concluded about the solution to the system Ax = 0?
options: There are infinitely many solutions forming a 10D space.
The system is inconsistent and has no solutions.
The only solution is the trivial solution (the zero vector).
The solution is a line passing through the origin.
questions.explanation: A 10x10 matrix with 10 pivots has a rank of 10. Since there are no free variables (10 columns - 10 pivots = 0), the null space has a dimension of zero, meaning only the zero vector is mapped to zero.
correctAnswers: The only solution is the trivial solution (the zero vector).

questions.prompt: Based on the simulation of the linear transformation, why does the null space appear as a line rather than just a single point at the origin?
options: Because the transformation maps every single vector in the input space to the origin.
Because one dimension of the input space is lost, meaning an entire direction of vectors is crushed to zero.
Because the matrix has a rank equal to the number of dimensions in the input space.
Because the transformation is a simple rotation that preserves all original vectors.
questions.explanation: When a matrix has a rank less than its input dimension, it 'collapses' space. If one dimension is lost, all vectors along that specific line (the null space) are moved to the zero vector by the transformation.

questions.prompt: If a linear transformation $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is known to be one-to-one (injective), which of the following must be true based on the Rank-Nullity Theorem?

The transformation is increasing the number of columns in the matrix, requiring more rank.
The domain itself is physically shrinking, leaving less 'stuff' to project into the codomain.
The rank and nullity are both increasing simultaneously to compensate for the change in orientation.

questions.prompt: Consider a 4x2 matrix A representing 4 observations across 2 features. What is the dimensions (shape) of its transpose, A^T, and what does this transformation represent in the context of the data?
options: 4x2; it keeps the observations as rows but reorders the features.
2x4; it treats the original features as observations and the observations as features.
2x2; it reduces the data to only the feature-to-feature relationships.
4x4; it expands the data to show how every observation relates to every other observation.
questions.explanation: Transposing a matrix swaps its rows and columns. For a 4x2 matrix, the 4 rows become 4 columns and the 2 columns become 2 rows, resulting in a 2x4 shape where the roles of observations and features are inverted.
correctAnswers: 2x4; it treats the original features as observations and the observations as features.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements correctly describe properties of symmetric matrices?
options: The element at index (i, j) must be equal to the element at index (j, i).
A symmetric matrix must always be square.
The elements on the main diagonal must all be zero.
A matrix is symmetric if and only if A = -A^T.
The main diagonal acts as the axis of symmetry for the off-diagonal elements.
questions.explanation: Symmetry requires the matrix to be square so that A and A^T have the same dimensions. The definition A = A^T implies that elements across the main diagonal (the 'spine') must mirror each other, meaning index (i, j) equals index (j, i).
correctAnswers: The element at index (i, j) must be equal to the element at index (j, i).
A symmetric matrix must always be square.
The main diagonal acts as the axis of symmetry for the off-diagonal elements.

questions.prompt: If a square matrix A is skew-symmetric, what must be true about the entries on its main diagonal?
options: They must all be equal to 1.
They must all be equal to 0.
They can be any real number as long as they are equal to each other.
They must be the negative of the entries in the first row.
questions.explanation: In a skew-symmetric matrix, A^T = -A, which implies that for diagonal elements, a_ii = -a_ii. The only real number that satisfies this condition is zero.
correctAnswers: They must all be equal to 0.

questions.prompt: Any square matrix M can be decomposed into a symmetric part (S) and a skew-symmetric part (K). Which of the following formulas correctly identify these components?
options: S = M * M^T
K = M^T - M
M = S + K
questions.explanation: The symmetric part is the average of the matrix and its transpose, while the skew-symmetric part is half the difference. Adding these two components results back in the original matrix M.
correctAnswers: M = S + K

questions.prompt: Observe the transformation of the matrix grid. Why does the product of a matrix and its transpose always result in a symmetric shape, regardless of the original matrix's proportions?
options: Because the operation squares every individual element in the matrix, removing all negative signs.
Because the multiplication effectively 'dots' each row with every other row, ensuring the interaction between row i and row j is identical to row j and row i.
Because the transpose operation rotates the matrix 90 degrees clockwise, which cancels out any existing asymmetry.
Because the product of two non-square matrices always results in a diagonal matrix where all off-diagonal elements are zero.
questions.explanation: When calculating A multiplied by A^T, the entry at (i, j) is the dot product of row i of A and column j of A^T (which is row j of A). Since the dot product is commutative, the entry at (j, i) will be the same, creating symmetry.

questions.prompt: If a matrix $Q$ is orthogonal, why is the calculation of its inverse considered a 'computational shortcut' in high-speed graphics?
options: Because the inverse is simply the transpose of the matrix, requiring no complex row reduction.
Because orthogonal matrices are always diagonal, making inversion a simple reciprocal of terms.
Because the determinant of an orthogonal matrix is always zero, simplifying the adjugate formula.
Because orthogonal matrices only contain integers, which speeds up binary arithmetic.
questions.explanation: For an orthogonal matrix $Q$, the property $Q^T Q = I$ implies that $Q^{-1} = Q^T$. Transposing a matrix is a simple index swap that is far less computationally expensive than Gauss-Jordan elimination or other inversion algorithms.
correctAnswers: Because the inverse is simply the transpose of the matrix, requiring no complex row reduction.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conditions must be satisfied for a square matrix $Q$ to be classified as an orthogonal matrix?
options: Every column vector must have a magnitude (length) of exactly 1.
The dot product of any two distinct column vectors must be 0.
The determinant of the matrix must be either +1 or -1.
The matrix must be symmetric, meaning $Q = Q^T$.
The matrix must contain at least one row of zeros.
questions.explanation: Orthogonal matrices require orthonormal columns (unit length and mutually perpendicular). This geometric rigidity also forces the determinant to be ±1, representing a rotation or a reflection.
correctAnswers: Every column vector must have a magnitude (length) of exactly 1.
The dot product of any two distinct column vectors must be 0.
The determinant of the matrix must be either +1 or -1.

questions.prompt: In the context of rigid body motions, a transformation that preserves distances and angles but flips the 'handedness' of space (resulting in a determinant of -1) is specifically known as a ____.
questions.explanation: While both rotations and reflections are orthogonal, rotations preserve orientation (det = +1), whereas reflections invert it (det = -1).
correctAnswers: reflection
mirroring
householder transformation

questions.prompt: Consider a 2x2 matrix with columns $u = [1/\sqrt{2}, 1/\sqrt{2}]^T$ and $v = [1/\sqrt{2}, -1/\sqrt{2}]^T$. What is the primary reason this matrix is orthogonal?
options: The columns are unit vectors and their dot product is zero.
The matrix has a determinant of zero, meaning it collapses space.
All elements in the matrix are equal in absolute value.
The matrix is a diagonal matrix with ones on the main diagonal.
questions.explanation: To be orthogonal, the columns must be orthonormal. Here, $\|u\| = \sqrt{(1/2) + (1/2)} = 1$ and $u \cdot v = (1/2) - (1/2) = 0$.
correctAnswers: The columns are unit vectors and their dot product is zero.

questions.prompt: As the transformation matrix is applied to the grid, why do the shapes remain exactly the same size despite rotating around the origin?

Because the determinant of the matrix is 0, which prevents the area from expanding or contracting during motion.
Because the matrix is identity-based, meaning it can only swap the x and y coordinates without moving them.
questions.explanation: Orthogonal transformations preserve the 'fabric' of space; specifically, because $(Qx) · (Qy) = x · y$, the lengths of vectors and the angles between them do not change.

questions.prompt: Which property of diagonal matrices explains why they are considered the 'simplest' representation of a linear transformation?
options: They only contain prime numbers along the main diagonal.
They scale each coordinate axis independently without any 'mixing' or shearing.
They are always invertible regardless of the values on the diagonal.
They represent transformations that rotate space by 90 degrees.
questions.explanation: In a diagonal matrix, each entry on the diagonal corresponds to a specific axis. Since all off-diagonal entries are zero, the transformation of one coordinate doesn't depend on the others, avoiding the 'mixing' seen in dense matrices.
correctAnswers: They scale each coordinate axis independently without any 'mixing' or shearing.

questions.prompt: Consider two diagonal matrices, A and B, of the same dimension. Which of the following statements about their arithmetic are true?
options: The product AB is also a diagonal matrix.
The product AB is found by multiplying corresponding diagonal entries.
The inverse of A exists only if all diagonal entries are non-zero.
The product AB is generally different from the product BA.
The sum A + B results in a dense matrix if A and B have different values.
questions.explanation: Diagonal matrix multiplication is commutative (AB=BA) and results in another diagonal matrix where each entry is the product of the corresponding diagonal elements. An inverse exists if and only if no diagonal entry is zero, as the inverse entries are the reciprocals (1/x).
correctAnswers: The product AB is also a diagonal matrix.
The product AB is found by multiplying corresponding diagonal entries.
The inverse of A exists only if all diagonal entries are non-zero.

questions.prompt: The efficient process used to solve an upper triangular system by starting from the bottom-most variable and working upwards is called ____.
questions.explanation: Back-substitution is used for upper triangular matrices because the last equation contains only one variable, which once solved, can be plugged into the equation above it to solve the next variable, and so on.
correctAnswers: back-substitution
back substitution
backward substitution

questions.prompt: In an upper triangular matrix (U), where are the non-zero entries allowed to be located?
options: Only in the four corners of the matrix.
Only on the main diagonal and the entries above it.
Only on the main diagonal and the entries below it.
Strictly in the first row and first column.
questions.explanation: An upper triangular matrix has all zeros below the main diagonal. This 'staircase' structure means the equations are ordered such that the complexity of each equation increases as you move from the bottom to the top.
correctAnswers: Only on the main diagonal and the entries above it.

questions.prompt: As the animation processes the system of equations, why does the 'falling domino' effect allow for such a fast solution?
options: Because the diagonal entries are always equal to 1, eliminating the need for division.
Because the zeros in the lower-left ensure that each step only requires solving for a single unknown at a time.
Because the matrix is being converted into a dense matrix to utilize all available processors.
Because the animation shows the variables being solved simultaneously in a single parallel step.

sessions.title: Block Matrices and the LU Factorization

questions.prompt: Why is the LU factorization preferred over computing the matrix inverse A⁻¹ when solving multiple systems with the same matrix A but different vectors b?
options: Computing the inverse is computationally more expensive and less numerically stable than LU factorization.
The inverse of a matrix only exists if the matrix is already in upper triangular form.
LU factorization is the only way to handle matrices that have more than three rows.
The LU method requires only one step to solve for x, whereas the inverse requires three.
questions.explanation: Calculating the inverse is roughly three times more expensive than LU factorization and can introduce significant rounding errors. LU allows us to solve systems efficiently via forward and back substitution.
correctAnswers: Computing the inverse is computationally more expensive and less numerically stable than LU factorization.

image.alt: Diagram showing A = LU where L is lower triangular and U is upper triangular.

questions.prompt: When performing a standard LU decomposition without row swaps, which of the following statements about the resulting matrices L and U are true?
options: L is a lower triangular matrix with 1s on its main diagonal.
U is the final upper triangular matrix produced by Gaussian elimination.
The elements of L are the 'multipliers' used to create zeros in the lower part of A.
L and U always have the same values on their respective diagonals.
The product LU must equal the original matrix A.
questions.explanation: L records the history of row operations (multipliers), and its diagonal is fixed at 1. U is the echelon form. Their product reconstructs A.
correctAnswers: L is a lower triangular matrix with 1s on its main diagonal.
U is the final upper triangular matrix produced by Gaussian elimination.
The elements of L are the 'multipliers' used to create zeros in the lower part of A.
The product LU must equal the original matrix A.

questions.prompt: In the context of the LU decomposition, how should one interpret the matrix L?
options: It is the identity matrix modified by the cumulative record of the elimination steps.
It represents the final simplified state of the system after all variables are solved.
It is a diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues of the original system.
It is a matrix that stores the inverse of the final upper triangular result.
questions.explanation: L captures the 'DNA' of the elimination process by storing the multipliers in the specific positions where they were used to eliminate entries.
correctAnswers: It is the identity matrix modified by the cumulative record of the elimination steps.

questions.prompt: Under what conditions can you treat sub-sections of a matrix as 'blocks' for the purpose of block multiplication?
options: The inner dimensions of the blocks must align, similar to scalar matrix multiplication.
The blocks must all be square matrices of the same size.
The partitioning of the columns of the first matrix must match the partitioning of the rows of the second.
Blocks can only be used if the resulting product matrix is also lower triangular.
questions.explanation: Block multiplication mirrors standard multiplication, so the 'columns' of the left-side blocks must match the 'rows' of the right-side blocks for the operation to be defined.
correctAnswers: The inner dimensions of the blocks must align, similar to scalar matrix multiplication.
The partitioning of the columns of the first matrix must match the partitioning of the rows of the second.

questions.prompt: Observe the process of transforming matrix A into its LU components. Why does the complexity of the operation remain lower than calculating a full matrix inverse?
options: Because the zeros in the triangular forms eliminate the need for most multiplication and addition steps during substitution.
Because the LU process ignores the values in the right-hand side vector b until the very end.
Because the algorithm only processes the diagonal elements, leaving the rest of the matrix unchanged.
Because lower triangular matrices are automatically considered solved without any further calculation.
questions.explanation: The simulation shows that as we produce zeros in U and record multipliers in L, the structure of these matrices allows us to bypass the massive number of operations required to fully invert a dense matrix.

sessions.title: Determinants as Signed Area and Volume

questions.prompt: If a 2D transformation matrix has a determinant of 3, what happens to the area of a circle with an initial area of 5 square units after the transformation is applied?
options: The area becomes 15 square units.
The area remains 5 square units.
The area becomes 8 square units.
The area becomes 1.66 square units.
questions.explanation: The determinant acts as a uniform scaling factor for area across the entire plane. Since the determinant is 3, any shape—regardless of its geometry—will have its area multiplied by 3.
correctAnswers: The area becomes 15 square units.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements accurately describe a 3x3 matrix with a determinant of 0?
options: The transformation collapses the 3D space into a 2D plane, a 1D line, or a point.
The volume of any shape transformed by this matrix will be zero.
The matrix can be inverted to restore the original 3D volume.
The column vectors of the matrix are linearly dependent.
The transformation preserves the orientation of the original basis vectors.
questions.explanation: A zero determinant indicates a loss of dimensionality (collapse), meaning all volumes become zero. Because information is lost during this collapse, the process is not invertible.
correctAnswers: The transformation collapses the 3D space into a 2D plane, a 1D line, or a point.
The volume of any shape transformed by this matrix will be zero.
The column vectors of the matrix are linearly dependent.

questions.prompt: In linear algebra, a negative determinant indicates that the transformation has changed the ____ of the space.
questions.explanation: While the absolute value of the determinant tells us the scaling factor, the sign tells us if the space has been flipped or mirrored, which is referred to as its orientation.
correctAnswers: orientation
handedness
relative orientation

image.alt: A unit cube transformed into a smaller parallelepiped representing a volume scale factor of 0.5.

questions.prompt: If you transform a unit cube using a 3x3 matrix and the resulting volume is 0.5, what is the determinant of that matrix?
questions.explanation: The determinant of a 3x3 matrix is exactly equal to the volume of the parallelepiped formed by its column vectors, which is the same as the factor by which the volume of a unit cube is scaled.

questions.prompt: As one vector is rotated to become perfectly aligned with the other, why does the determinant value approach and eventually reach zero?
options: Because the scaling factor for area decreases as the two-dimensional shape flattens into a one-dimensional line.
Because the lengths of the individual vectors are decreasing until they have no magnitude.
Because the transformation is switching from a right-handed system to a left-handed system.
Because the matrix entries are being multiplied by zero during the rotation process.
questions.explanation: The determinant measures the area of the parallelogram formed by the vectors. As the vectors become collinear, the 'height' of the parallelogram relative to its base disappears, resulting in a 1D line with zero 2D area.

correctAnswers: Because the scaling factor for area decreases as the two-dimensional shape flattens into a one-dimensional line.

questions.prompt: When calculating the determinant of a 3x3 matrix, what is the primary purpose of finding the 'Minor' of a specific element?
options: To reduce the 3x3 matrix into a 2x2 'sub-view' by ignoring that element's row and column.
To determine whether the final determinant value will be positive or negative.
To identify which row contains the most zeros for efficient calculation.
To multiply the entire matrix by a scaling factor to simplify the numbers.
questions.explanation: A minor is the determinant of the smaller matrix that remains after you 'ignore' or cross out the row and column of a specific element, allowing for a recursive reduction of the problem.
correctAnswers: To reduce the 3x3 matrix into a 2x2 'sub-view' by ignoring that element's row and column.

questions.prompt: Which of the following factors determine the sign (positive or negative) of a cofactor in the Laplace expansion?
options: The numerical value of the element itself (positive or negative).
The element's position within the alternating 'chessboard' pattern of signs.
The parity of the sum of the row index and column index (i + j).
Whether the matrix has a determinant of zero.
The orientation of the sub-space being measured.
questions.explanation: Cofactor signs are determined by position (row + column index), which acts as an orientation tracker. The sign is independent of the element's actual value or the total determinant.
correctAnswers: The element's position within the alternating 'chessboard' pattern of signs.
The parity of the sum of the row index and column index (i + j).
The orientation of the sub-space being measured.

questions.prompt: To minimize calculation steps in cofactor expansion, a learner should look for the row or column with the most ____.
questions.explanation: Expanding along a row or column with zeros is the 'path of least resistance' because any term multiplied by zero is eliminated, reducing the number of minors you need to calculate.
correctAnswers: zeros
0s
zeroes

questions.prompt: If you are expanding a 4x4 matrix using the Laplace method, how many 3x3 determinants must you theoretically calculate in the first step?
questions.explanation: Laplace expansion is recursive; a 4x4 determinant is the sum of 4 weighted 3x3 determinants (minors). If the chosen row/column contains zeros, some of these calculations may be skipped.

questions.prompt: As the animation processes the expansion of a 3x3 matrix containing a zero, why does the calculation 'skip' one of the branches?
options: Because the zero element acts as a multiplier of zero for that entire minor's contribution.
Because the minor associated with a zero element is automatically equal to zero.
Because the chessboard sign for any position containing a zero is neutral.
Because the matrix must be rearranged to move all zeros to the top row first.
questions.explanation: The cofactor expansion formula multiplies the element by its minor and its sign. If the element is 0, the product is 0 regardless of the minor's value, allowing us to ignore that branch of calculation.
questions.animationHtml: Animation of Cofactor Expansion across the first row of a 3x3 matrix
correctAnswers: Because the zero element acts as a multiplier of zero for that entire minor's contribution.

questions.prompt: Suppose you have a 3x3 matrix A and you create a new matrix B by multiplying every entry in A by a scalar k. What is the determinant of B in terms of the determinant of A?
options: det(B) = k * det(A)
det(B) = k^2 * det(A)
det(B) = k^3 * det(A)
det(B) = 3k * det(A)
questions.explanation: Since the determinant scales linearly with each row, multiplying a 3x3 matrix by k scales each of the three rows by k. Thus, the total effect is multiplying the determinant by k once for each row, resulting in k cubed.
correctAnswers: det(B) = k^3 * det(A)

questions.prompt: Which of the following elementary row operations will result in a matrix with a determinant that is different from the original matrix?
options: Swapping the first row with the second row
Adding 5 times the third row to the second row
Multiplying the entire third row by -1
Multiplying the first row by 2 and adding it to the fourth row
Multiplying every entry in the first row by 0.5
questions.explanation: Row swaps multiply the determinant by -1, and scaling a row multiplies the determinant by that scale factor. Adding a multiple of one row to another (shear) is the only operation listed that preserves the determinant value exactly.
correctAnswers: Swapping the first row with the second row
Multiplying the entire third row by -1
Multiplying every entry in the first row by 0.5

questions.prompt: If a 4x4 matrix is reduced to upper triangular form using only row replacements and exactly three row swaps, the determinant of the original matrix is equal to ____ times the product of the diagonal entries of the triangular matrix.
correctAnswers: negative one

questions.prompt: Why is the determinant of an upper triangular matrix simply the product of its diagonal entries?
options: Because the area of the shape is zero if there are any non-zero values below the diagonal.
Because the matrix can be viewed as a hyper-rectangle where the diagonal entries represent the lengths of the orthogonal axes.
Because row swaps are not allowed when forming triangular matrices.
Because the cofactor expansion along the first column repeatedly reduces to the next diagonal element.
questions.explanation: Using cofactor expansion on an upper triangular matrix, every step involves a column with only one non-zero entry (the diagonal). This systematically reduces the problem to the product of those diagonal entries.
correctAnswers: Because the cofactor expansion along the first column repeatedly reduces to the next diagonal element.

questions.prompt: While watching the transformation of the unit square, why does the area remain constant during the 'shearing' phase even though the shape is tilting?
options: Because the lengths of all four sides of the parallelogram remain unchanged during the tilt.
Because the base length and the perpendicular height of the shape remain constant throughout the transformation.
Because a row swap occurs simultaneously to balance the change in orientation.
Because the scaling factor of the vertical axis is the reciprocal of the horizontal tilt.
questions.explanation: In a shear (adding a multiple of one row to another), the 'base' along one axis stays the same and the 'height' relative to that base doesn't change, so the area (base x height) is invariant.

questions.prompt: Suppose you have a 2x2 matrix $A$ that stretches a shape's area by a factor of 4, and a matrix $B$ that shrinks it by a factor of 0.5. What is the determinant of the product $AB$?
questions.explanation: According to the product rule, $det(AB) = det(A)det(B)$. Since the determinant represents the scaling factor, we calculate $4 \times 0.5 = 2$.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements regarding the relationship between a matrix $A$ and its inverse $A^{-1}$ are true?
options: The product of their determinants must equal 1.
If $det(A) = 0.2$, then $det(A^{-1}) = 5$.
The inverse exists even if the determinant of A is zero.
The determinant of the identity matrix $I$ is the sum of $det(A)$ and $det(A^{-1})$.
Geometrically, $A^{-1}$ must reverse the scaling effect of $A$.
questions.explanation: Since $AA^{-1} = I$, and $det(I) = 1$, the product rule implies $det(A)det(A^{-1}) = 1$. This means $det(A^{-1}) = 1/det(A)$, and an inverse can only exist if $det(A) \neq 0$.
correctAnswers: The product of their determinants must equal 1.
If $det(A) = 0.2$, then $det(A^{-1}) = 5$.
Geometrically, $A^{-1}$ must reverse the scaling effect of $A$.

questions.prompt: If a transformation represented by matrix $M$ flattens a 3D volume into a 2D plane, its determinant is equal to ____.
correctAnswers: zero

questions.prompt: Given a matrix $A$ where $det(A) = 5$, what is the determinant of $A^3$ (the product $AAA$)?
questions.explanation: Using the product rule $det(AB) = det(A)det(B)$ repeatedly, $det(AAA) = det(A) \times det(A) \times det(A)$, which is $5^3 = 125$.

Because the collapse to a lower dimension destroys the information needed to map points back to their original locations.
Because the scaling factor is a negative value, which reverses the orientation of the axes.
Because the transformation increases the area so much that the inverse would require division by an infinite value.
questions.explanation: When the determinant is zero, space is 'flattened' (e.g., a plane into a line). Multiple different points in the original space are squashed into the same point, making it impossible to uniquely 'undo' the operation.

questions.prompt: Why does the set of all polynomials of degree *exactly* 2 fail to be a vector space under standard addition?
options: It lacks an additive identity because the zero polynomial has no degree.
It is not closed under addition because the sum of two degree-2 polynomials can result in a lower degree.
It fails the commutativity axiom because the order of polynomial addition matters.
Polynomials are functions, and vector space axioms only apply to geometric arrows.
questions.explanation: Closure requires that the result of an operation stays within the set. If you add x² and -x²+x, the x² terms cancel, leaving a degree-1 polynomial, which is outside the set of 'exactly degree 2' polynomials.
correctAnswers: It is not closed under addition because the sum of two degree-2 polynomials can result in a lower degree.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are 'Closure' axioms that a set must satisfy to be considered a vector space?
options: The sum of any two elements in the set must also be in the set.
The product of any two elements in the set must also be in the set.
Multiplying any element in the set by a real scalar must result in an element within the set.
Every element must have a corresponding multiplicative inverse within the set.
questions.explanation: A vector space requires closure under addition and closure under scalar multiplication. It does not require closure under 'vector multiplication' (like the dot product), nor does it require multiplicative inverses for the vectors themselves.
correctAnswers: The sum of any two elements in the set must also be in the set.
Multiplying any element in the set by a real scalar must result in an element within the set.

questions.prompt: Consider the set of all integers. Why does this set fail to be a vector space over the field of real numbers (ℝ)?
options: The set of integers does not contain an additive identity.
The set of integers is not closed under standard addition.
Scaling an integer by a non-integer real number (like 0.5) results in a value outside the set.
Integers cannot be represented as coordinates in a 2D plane.
questions.explanation: While integers are closed under addition, a vector space over ℝ must be closed under multiplication by *any* real scalar. Since 0.5 * 5 = 2.5 (not an integer), the set fails the scalar multiplication closure axiom.
correctAnswers: Scaling an integer by a non-integer real number (like 0.5) results in a value outside the set.

image.alt: Diagram showing different mathematical objects being tested against the ten axioms to see if they qualify as a vector space.

questions.prompt: If a mathematical structure is proven to satisfy all ten vector space axioms, which of the following statements become true?
options: We can apply linear algebra theorems, such as those regarding span and basis, to that structure.
The elements of the set must be representable as column matrices.
The set must contain a 'zero' element that acts as an additive identity.
The set is restricted to three dimensions or fewer.
questions.explanation: The power of abstraction is that any set satisfying the axioms (including the existence of a zero element) inherits all the properties and theorems of linear algebra, regardless of whether the elements are functions, matrices, or arrows.
correctAnswers: We can apply linear algebra theorems, such as those regarding span and basis, to that structure.
The set must contain a 'zero' element that acts as an additive identity.

questions.prompt: Based on the observed behavior of the polynomial set as the coefficients change, why does 'closure under addition' fail specifically for polynomials of degree exactly 'n'?
options: Because the leading coefficients can sum to zero, effectively reducing the degree of the resulting polynomial.
Because adding two polynomials always increases the degree beyond the limit of the space.
Because the additive identity (the zero polynomial) is technically a polynomial of degree zero, not degree n.
Because the sum of two continuous curves may result in a discontinuous function that is no longer a polynomial.
questions.explanation: In the simulation, when the leading terms (like 2x² and -2x²) cancel out, the result is a lower-degree polynomial. This means the operation 'landed' outside the set of polynomials of degree exactly n, violating closure.

questions.prompt: Why is a line in R^2 that does not pass through the origin disqualified from being a subspace?
options: It lacks a zero vector and is not closed under addition or scalar multiplication.
It is finite in length, which violates the axiom of infinite extent.
A line is a one-dimensional object and subspaces must be two-dimensional.
The vectors on the line are linearly dependent on the axes.
questions.explanation: A subspace must contain the zero vector (the origin). Furthermore, if you add two vectors from a shifted line, the result 'jumps' off the line, and scaling a vector by zero would result in the origin, which is not on the line, violating closure.
correctAnswers: It lacks a zero vector and is not closed under addition or scalar multiplication.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conditions must be verified to prove that a subset S is a subspace of a vector space V?
options: The zero vector of V is in S.
The sum of any two vectors in S remains in S.
Any vector in S can be expressed as a unit vector.
The product of any scalar and any vector in S remains in S.
S must contain the same number of elements as V.
questions.explanation: These are the 'big three' requirements of the Subspace Test. Since S is inside a vector space, properties like commutativity and associativity are inherited automatically; only membership and closure must be checked.
correctAnswers: The zero vector of V is in S.
The sum of any two vectors in S remains in S.
The product of any scalar and any vector in S remains in S.

questions.prompt: The set of all possible linear combinations of a collection of vectors is known as their ____.
questions.explanation: The span is the 'recipe book' that generates a subspace by taking every possible combination of scaling and adding the given vectors.

questions.prompt: Consider the first quadrant of R^2 (where x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0). Why does this subset fail to be a subspace?
options: It is not closed under scalar multiplication because multiplying by a negative scalar exits the quadrant.
It does not contain the zero vector.
It is not closed under addition because adding two positive vectors can yield a negative result.
The set is bounded by the axes and therefore cannot be a vector space.
questions.explanation: While the first quadrant contains the zero vector and is closed under addition, multiplying a vector like (1, 1) by -1 results in (-1, -1), which is in the third quadrant, failing the closure test.
correctAnswers: It is not closed under scalar multiplication because multiplying by a negative scalar exits the quadrant.

questions.prompt: What causes the resulting shape to change from a 1D line to a 2D plane as the second vector is adjusted?
options: The change occurs because the two vectors become linearly independent, allowing their span to cover a higher-dimensional area.
The change occurs because the magnitude of the second vector increases beyond a specific threshold value.
The change occurs because the vectors are being added together rather than being multiplied by scalars.
The change occurs because the zero vector is removed from the set, allowing the span to expand.
questions.explanation: When vectors are parallel (linearly dependent), their span is just a line. As soon as the second vector points in a different direction, their linear combinations can reach any point in the plane they define.

questions.prompt: Why is the 'uniqueness' of the scalars in the coordinate representation $x = c_1v_1 + \dots + c_nv_n$ essential for defining a coordinate vector?
options: It ensures that every vector in the space can be represented by at least one list of numbers.
It prevents a single vector from having multiple 'addresses' relative to the same basis, ensuring a well-defined mapping.
It guarantees that the basis vectors are all of unit length, simplifying future calculations.
It allows us to change the order of the basis vectors without changing the coordinate vector.
questions.explanation: Uniqueness ensures that the mapping from a vector to its coordinate representation is a function; without it, calculations would be ambiguous because one vector could correspond to different numerical lists.
correctAnswers: It prevents a single vector from having multiple 'addresses' relative to the same basis, ensuring a well-defined mapping.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements correctly describe the relationship between a vector $x$ and its coordinate vector $[x]_B$ relative to a basis $B = \{v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n\}$?
options: The coordinate vector is an ordered list; changing the sequence of vectors in $B$ will generally change $[x]_B$.
The coordinate vector $[x]_B$ always has the same entries as $x$ regardless of the basis chosen.
The entries of $[x]_B$ are the weights used in a linear combination of the basis vectors to produce $x$.
Finding $[x]_B$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ relative to a non-standard basis typically requires solving a system of linear equations.
A vector $x$ can only have a coordinate vector if it is an element of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
questions.explanation: Coordinates are weights for a specific ordered set of basis vectors. For non-standard bases, we must solve $x = P_B[x]_B$ to find these weights.
correctAnswers: The coordinate vector is an ordered list; changing the sequence of vectors in $B$ will generally change $[x]_B$.
The entries of $[x]_B$ are the weights used in a linear combination of the basis vectors to produce $x$.
Finding $[x]_B$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ relative to a non-standard basis typically requires solving a system of linear equations.

questions.prompt: In the vector space $P_2$ (polynomials of degree at most 2), the coordinate vector of $p(t) = 5 - 2t + 7t^2$ relative to the standard basis $B = \{1, t, t^2\}$ is written as the column vector ____.
questions.explanation: Relative to the standard basis of polynomials, the coordinates are simply the coefficients of the polynomial terms in the order of the basis elements.

questions.prompt: Consider a vector $x$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and two different bases, $B_1$ and $B_2$. If $x$ remains stationary, why do its coordinates change when we switch from $B_1$ to $B_2$?
options: Because the vector $x$ physically moves to a new location in the plane when the basis changes.
Because the coordinates represent the vector's relationship to the 'grid' defined by the basis, and the grid has been redefined.
Because the magnitude of the vector $x$ is recalculated using a different distance formula for each basis.
Because the number of dimensions in the coordinate vector must match the number of vectors in the new basis.
questions.explanation: Coordinates are relative measurements. Just as a distance can be '1' in meters or '100' in centimeters, the same vector is described by different scalars depending on the 'units' (basis vectors) used.
correctAnswers: Because the coordinates represent the vector's relationship to the 'grid' defined by the basis, and the grid has been redefined.

questions.prompt: As the basis vectors are adjusted from an orthogonal (perpendicular) orientation to a nearly parallel (highly skewed) orientation, why do the coordinate values for the fixed point change so drastically?

The point is being moved by the basis vectors, requiring higher scalars to reach the new physical location in space.
To reach the same point using vectors that point in nearly the same direction, the 'weights' must become much larger to compensate for the loss of independent coverage.
The coordinate system is collapsing into a lower dimension, which requires the third coordinate to absorb the values of the first two.
questions.explanation: When basis vectors are nearly parallel, they are 'less efficient' at covering the space. To reach a point that has a component perpendicular to them, very large positive and negative combinations are required.

The grid lines used to measure the vector.
The identity of the vector as an abstract geometric object.

questions.prompt: In the context of Cramer's Rule, what does it mean geometrically when we replace the $i$-th column of matrix $A$ with the output vector $b$ to find $x_i$?
options: We are calculating the total area of the parallelogram formed by all columns except $b$.
We are finding the ratio of the volume of a 'mutated' parallelepiped to the volume of the original one.
We are determining if the output vector $b$ is perpendicular to the columns of $A$.
We are shifting the entire coordinate system so that $b$ becomes the new origin.
questions.explanation: Cramer's Rule interprets the value of a variable as the scaling factor between the original determinant (volume) and the determinant of a matrix where one column is substituted by the target vector $b$.
correctAnswers: We are finding the ratio of the volume of a 'mutated' parallelepiped to the volume of the original one.

questions.prompt: Under which of the following conditions is Cramer's Rule considered an inappropriate or impossible choice for solving a linear system $Ax = b$?
options: The determinant of the coefficient matrix $A$ is zero.
The system is a large $100 \times 100$ sparse matrix used in a high-speed simulation.
The system consists of only two variables and two equations.
The output vector $b$ is the zero vector.
The matrix $A$ is non-square (more equations than variables).
questions.explanation: Cramer's Rule fails if $\det(A)=0$ (division by zero) and is only defined for square matrices. While mathematically valid for large systems, it is computationally inefficient compared to Gaussian elimination for high-order matrices.
correctAnswers: The determinant of the coefficient matrix $A$ is zero.
The system is a large $100 \times 100$ sparse matrix used in a high-speed simulation.
The matrix $A$ is non-square (more equations than variables).

questions.prompt: If a $2 \times 2$ system has $\det(A) = 5$ and the determinant of the matrix formed by replacing the second column with $b$ is $15$, then the value of $y$ (the second variable) is ____.
questions.explanation: According to the formula $x_i = \det(A_i) / \det(A)$, we divide the 'mutated' determinant by the original determinant: $15 / 5 = 3$.
correctAnswers: three

questions.prompt: If the determinant of the coefficient matrix is exactly zero, what does this indicate about the relationship between the columns of $A$ and the vector $b$?
options: The columns of $A$ span the entire space, but $b$ is the zero vector.
The columns of $A$ are linearly independent.
The 'volume' of the transformation has collapsed, meaning the system is either inconsistent or has infinite solutions.
Cramer's Rule can still be used if we use the absolute value of the determinant.
questions.explanation: A zero determinant means the matrix is singular (not invertible), implying the geometric volume is flat and the system lacks a unique solution.
correctAnswers: The 'volume' of the transformation has collapsed, meaning the system is either inconsistent or has infinite solutions.

questions.prompt: Watch the transformation as the output vector $b$ moves closer to one of the basis columns of $A$. Why does the value of that specific variable $x_i$ approach 1 while others approach 0?
options: Because the area of the mutated parallelogram becomes identical to the area of the original parallelogram when $b$ aligns with the column it replaced.
Because the determinant of a matrix always increases when $b$ is at a 45-degree angle to the origin.
Because the division by $\det(A)$ is bypassed when the vector $b$ has a length of exactly one.
Because the system performs a Gaussian elimination step automatically when $b$ is a unit vector.
questions.explanation: When $b$ is identical to the $i$-th column, the 'mutated' matrix $A_i$ becomes identical to $A$, making the ratio $\det(A)/\det(A) = 1$.

sessions.title: The Adjugate and the Inverse Formula

questions.prompt: Which step distinguishes the formation of the adjugate matrix from the formation of the matrix of cofactors?
options: Calculating the determinant of each submatrix
Applying the checkerboard sign pattern to each minor
Transposing the matrix of cofactors
Dividing each entry by the overall determinant
questions.explanation: The adjugate (or adjoint) is specifically defined as the transpose of the cofactor matrix. Calculating sub-determinants and applying signs creates the cofactor matrix itself, while dividing by the determinant produces the inverse matrix.
correctAnswers: Transposing the matrix of cofactors

questions.prompt: According to the relationship $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = \det(A)I$, what occurs when a matrix $A$ is multiplied by its adjugate?
options: The off-diagonal entries resulting from the multiplication are always zero.
The diagonal entries of the product are all equal to the determinant of A.
The resulting matrix is always the Identity matrix $I$, regardless of the determinant.
The operation is equivalent to the Laplace expansion of the determinant along rows or columns.
The product results in a scalar value rather than a matrix.
questions.explanation: The identity $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = \det(A)I$ shows that the product is a diagonal matrix where every diagonal element is $\det(A)$. This happens because the dot product of a row with its own cofactors gives the determinant, while the dot product with cofactors of a different row results in zero.
correctAnswers: The off-diagonal entries resulting from the multiplication are always zero.
The diagonal entries of the product are all equal to the determinant of A.
The operation is equivalent to the Laplace expansion of the determinant along rows or columns.
