questions.prompt: If you have a system of three linear equations representing three distinct planes in 3D space, which of the following geometric scenarios would result in 'no solution'?
options: Two planes are parallel to each other, while the third intersects both
The three planes intersect at exactly one shared point
The three planes intersect to form a triangular prism shape where they meet in pairs but never all three at once
All three planes are parallel and distinct from one another
The three planes intersect along a single common line
questions.explanation: A system has no solution if there is no point common to all equations. This happens if any two planes are parallel/distinct, or if they intersect in a way (like a prism) where no single point lies on all three surfaces simultaneously.
correctAnswers: Two planes are parallel to each other, while the third intersects both
The three planes intersect to form a triangular prism shape where they meet in pairs but never all three at once
All three planes are parallel and distinct from one another

questions.prompt: The vector that is perpendicular to every vector lying within a plane is known as the ____ vector.
questions.explanation: The normal vector defines the orientation of a plane in space. The dot product of the normal vector and any vector lying in the plane is always zero.
correctAnswers: normal
normal vector

questions.prompt: Given a point P on a plane and a normal vector n, what condition must a variable point X satisfy to lie on that plane?
options: The vector (X - P) must be parallel to n
The dot product of n and (X - P) must be zero
The length of vector X must be equal to the length of vector n
The sum of n and X must equal P
questions.explanation: If a point X is on the plane, the vector from P to X lies within the plane. By definition, the normal vector n is orthogonal to every vector in the plane, so their dot product must be zero.
correctAnswers: The dot product of n and (X - P) must be zero

questions.prompt: As the normal vector of the second plane is rotated to become perfectly parallel to the normal vector of the first plane (without the planes overlapping), why does the solution set suddenly become empty?
options: Because parallel normal vectors imply the planes now occupy the same space and are redundant.
Because as the normal vectors align, the line of intersection moves to infinity and the planes no longer share any points.
Because rotating a normal vector changes the dimension of the individual planes from 2D to 3D.
Because the dot product of the two normal vectors reaches its maximum value, preventing any intersection.

questions.prompt: In the QR decomposition A = QR, why is the matrix R always upper triangular?
options: Because the Gram-Schmidt process builds each column of Q from current and previous columns of A only.
Because each column j of A is constructed solely from the first j orthonormal vectors in Q.
Because orthogonal matrices must always be multiplied by triangular matrices to maintain stability.
Because the diagonal of R represents the eigenvalues of the original matrix A.
questions.explanation: The Gram-Schmidt process is incremental: the j-th column of A is a linear combination of the first j orthonormal basis vectors. This means A[,j] has no components in the direction of Q[,j+1] or beyond, forcing all entries in R below the diagonal (where row index > column index) to be zero.
correctAnswers: Because each column j of A is constructed solely from the first j orthonormal vectors in Q.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are true properties of the matrix Q in a QR decomposition?
options: The columns of Q are all unit vectors.
The columns of Q are mutually perpendicular (orthogonal).
The determinant of Q must always be 1.
The inverse of Q is equal to its transpose.
Q is always an upper triangular matrix.
questions.explanation: Q is an orthogonal matrix, meaning its columns form an orthonormal basis. Orthonormal vectors are both unit length and mutually perpendicular. For any orthogonal matrix, Q multiplied by its transpose equals the identity, so its inverse is its transpose.
correctAnswers: The columns of Q are all unit vectors.
The columns of Q are mutually perpendicular (orthogonal).
The inverse of Q is equal to its transpose.

questions.prompt: In the matrix R, the entry on the diagonal R[j,j] represents the ____ of the j-th orthogonal vector before it was normalized.

norm

questions.prompt: If you are performing a QR decomposition and find a non-zero value in the bottom-left entry of a 2x2 R matrix, what does this signify?
options: The decomposition is correct and the matrix A is simply non-invertible.
The first column of A contains a component of the second orthonormal vector from Q.
The vectors in A were already orthonormal before the process started.
The matrix Q has lost its orthogonality due to the magnitude of the diagonal entries.
questions.explanation: In an upper triangular matrix R, R[2,1] must be zero. If it is not, it implies that the first column of A requires the second 'future' basis vector to be reconstructed, which contradicts the incremental nature of the Gram-Schmidt process.
correctAnswers: The first column of A contains a component of the second orthonormal vector from Q.

questions.prompt: As the angle between the two original columns of matrix A decreases (making them nearly parallel), what accounts for the behavior of the diagonal entries in R compared to the off-diagonal entries?
options: The diagonal entries vanish because the vectors are becoming perfectly orthogonal to the basis.
The off-diagonal entry R[1,2] grows because the second vector's projection onto the first direction increases.
The diagonal entries grow significantly to compensate for the lack of independent directions in Q.
The matrix R becomes diagonal because nearly parallel vectors require no subtraction to orthogonalize.
questions.explanation: As vectors become more parallel, their 'overlap' or dot product increases. Since R[1,2] represents the projection of the second vector onto the first, this off-diagonal value grows as the vectors align.

sessions.title: Gaussian Elimination and Row Echelon Form

questions.prompt: During Gaussian elimination, what should be done if the current pivot position contains a zero and there are non-zero entries in the rows beneath it?
options: End the elimination process immediately
Multiply the entire row by zero to clear it
Perform a row swap with a lower row to move a non-zero entry into the pivot position
Skip that column and move to the next pivot position in the same row
questions.explanation: If a zero appears in a pivot position, you must swap it with a lower row that has a non-zero value in that column. This tactical maneuver prevents a 'division by zero' error and allows the elimination algorithm to continue downward.
correctAnswers: Perform a row swap with a lower row to move a non-zero entry into the pivot position

questions.prompt: Which of the following Elementary Row Operations are considered 'information-preserving' because they do not change the solution set of a system of equations?
options: Swapping any two rows
Multiplying a row by a non-zero scalar
Adding a multiple of one row to another row
Replacing a row with a row of zeros
Squaring all elements within a row
questions.explanation: The three legal operations—swapping, scaling by a non-zero constant, and adding a multiple of one row to another—maintain the equality of the system. Replacing a row with zeros or squaring elements destroys the specific linear relationship and changes the solution set.
correctAnswers: Swapping any two rows
Multiplying a row by a non-zero scalar
Adding a multiple of one row to another row

questions.prompt: The resulting 'staircase' shape of a matrix after Gaussian elimination, where each leading non-zero entry is to the right of the leading entry in the row above it, is called ____.
correctAnswers: Row Echelon Form
REF
echelon form

questions.prompt: In a 3x3 matrix that has been successfully reduced to Row Echelon Form, which row represents the 'simplest' equation to solve first during back-substitution?
options: The first (top) row
The third (bottom) row
The middle row
All rows are equally complex
questions.explanation: The bottom row is the simplest because it contains the most leading zeros, typically leaving only one variable to solve for directly (e.g., 2z = 4). You then use that value to work your way up the staircase.
correctAnswers: The third (bottom) row

questions.prompt: What does a 'zero' in a matrix represent in the context of solving a system of linear equations?
options: The total absence of a variable in that specific equation
An error in the original data set
A mathematical 'anchor' or pivot point
A simplification of the system's complexity
A point where two lines are parallel
questions.explanation: Zeros are our 'best friends' in linear algebra because they indicate that a variable no longer appears in a specific equation, reducing the complexity of the system and bringing us closer to a solution.
correctAnswers: The total absence of a variable in that specific equation
A simplification of the system's complexity
